plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 15.8.6
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a physical analogy for the curl of a vector field at a point. At the center is a labeled point P0, around which concentric dashed blue arcs indicate a circular fluid flow pattern. Four paddle-like rectangular surfaces (salmon-colored) radiate outward from P0 like propeller blades. A vertical spindle passes through P0, and the vector Curl F(P0) labels an upward arrow along the spindle, with a curved arrow showing the direction of rotation. The figure provides the physical interpretation that a small paddle wheel immersed in the fluid at P0 rotates most rapidly when its spindle is aligned with curl F(P0), establishing the connection between the curl vector and the direction of maximum circulation density.

elements: central point P0 drawn as a small black sphere with label 'P0'
vertical spindle (thin dark cylinder) passing through P0 along the world up-axis
curl vector arrow pointing up along the spindle, labeled 'Curl F(P0)' above it
curved rotation arrow wrapping around the upper spindle, indicating counterclockwise spin viewed from above
four salmon-colored rectangular paddle blades radiating from P0 at 90-degree intervals, each pitched like a propeller blade
three concentric circular flow arcs (light blue, broken/dashed) lying in the horizontal plane around the field center, representing the swirling fluid
small arrowheads on the flow arcs showing the counterclockwise circulation direction

interactions.teaches: The curl vector points along the paddle wheel's spin axis (right-hand rule); orbiting confirms the blades lie in the flow plane while Curl F(P0) is perpendicular to it

Curl is a local property of the field: dragging P0 away from the vortex center shrinks the curl vector, the paddle stops where the local circulation vanishes (r ~ 2.8), and beyond that the curl flips sign so the arrow points down and the wheel spins clockwise

interactions.label: Rotation rate
interactions.teaches: The magnitude of curl F at P0 equals twice the angular speed of the paddle wheel: raising the flow's rotation rate makes the blades spin faster and the curl arrow grow proportionally

demo_steps.title: Paddle wheel in the vortex
demo_steps.narration: At the field center the swirling flow catches the pitched blades and the wheel spins counterclockwise. The curl vector points straight up along the spindle — the axis of maximum circulation.

demo_steps.title: Weak circulation
demo_steps.narration: Lowering the rotation rate makes the paddle creep and the Curl F(P0) arrow shrink: curl measures the density of circulation, not the flow's speed at one point.

demo_steps.title: Strong circulation
demo_steps.narration: At a high rotation rate the blades whirl and the curl arrow stretches upward — its length is twice the paddle's angular speed.

demo_steps.title: Drag P0 off-center
demo_steps.narration: Now drag P0 outward across the fixed flow pattern. The spin slows, stops entirely near r = 2.8 where the local curl is zero, then reverses — the arrow flips downward and the wheel turns clockwise.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World: Y is up; the flow plane is the XZ plane at y = 0, scene spans about ±4.5 in X/Z and −0.5 to 2.5 in Y. Flow field is FIXED in world space, centered at the origin: three concentric broken circular arcs, radii 1.6, 2.4, 3.2, drawn as ~270-degree light-blue arcs (#6fb3d8, tube radius ~0.03) with small arrowheads indicating counterclockwise flow viewed from +Y. The paddle-wheel assembly is a single draggable Group whose origin is P0 (default at world origin): black sphere radius 0.12 labeled 'P0'; spindle = dark cylinder radius 0.035 from y = −0.25 to y = 1.5; curl arrow = shaft radius 0.05 plus cone head starting at y = 0, pointing +Y, label 'Curl F(P0)' floating above its tip; curved rotation arrow = black torus-arc radius 0.38 around the spindle at y ~ 1.55 with an arrowhead, CCW from above. Four blades: boxes 1.05 (radial length) x 0.02 x 0.55, centers at radius 0.62, azimuths 0/90/180/270 degrees, each pitched 30 degrees about its radial axis so the flow catches them; salmon fill #f2c1a7 with thin dark (#4a3a32) edges. Math for correctness: velocity field F(x,z) = S * exp(-(x^2+z^2)/8) * <−z, 0, x>, where S is the rotation-rate slider; curl at P0 is c = S * exp(-r^2/8) * (2 − r^2/4) in the +Y direction, zero at r = 2*sqrt(2) ~ 2.83, negative beyond. Set curl arrow length = 0.6*|c| (flip to −Y when c < 0) and paddle angular speed Ω = c/2 (sign included) so arrow length and spin speed always agree.
interactionPlan.notes: Structure the scene as: static flow-arc group at world origin + draggable paddle group. Implement dragPoint by raycasting the pointer onto the y = 0 plane and clamping the drag radius to <= 4; move the whole paddle group (sphere, spindle, blades, curl arrow, curved arrow) to the new P0. Each frame, recompute c from P0's XZ position and the slider value, then rotate the blade sub-group about local Y by Omega*dt and rescale/reorient the curl arrow (scale.y and 180-degree flip when c < 0); spin pauses automatically when the slider is 0. Render flow arcs as TubeGeometry arcs with gaps rather than dashed-line hacks so they read as the broken blue strokes in the source. Use HTML/sprite labels for 'P0' and 'Curl F(P0)' that always face the camera; keep the curved rotation arrow hidden or spinning with the blades for extra clarity.

authoredPrompt: This figure shows a physical analogy for the curl of a vector field at a point. At the center is a labeled point P0, around which concentric dashed blue arcs indicate a circular fluid flow pattern. Four paddle-like rectangular surfaces (salmon-colored) radiate outward from P0 like propeller blades. A vertical spindle passes through P0, and the vector Curl F(P0) labels an upward arrow along the spindle, with a curved arrow showing the direction of rotation. The figure provides the physical interpretation that a small paddle wheel immersed in the fluid at P0 rotates most rapidly when its spindle is aligned with curl F(P0), establishing the connection between the curl vector and the direction of maximum circulation density.
authoredInteractions:
- Drag point P₀ to a new location and display the updated Curl F(P₀) vector, showing how curl magnitude and direction vary across the field
- Slider for rotation rate: animate the paddle-wheel spinning and show how the curl vector magnitude corresponds to the angular speed of rotation
- Drag to rotate the 3D viewpoint to see the curl vector axis and paddle blades from any direction
authoredContext: We call curl F(P0) n the circulation density of F at P0 in the direction of n. This quantity has its maximum value when n is in the same direction as curl F(P0); this tells us that at each point in a steady-state fluid flow the maximum circulation density occurs in the direction of the curl. Physically, this means that if a small paddle wheel is immersed in the fluid so that the pivot point is at P0, then the paddles will turn most rapidly when the spindle is aligned with curl F(P0) (Figure 15.8.6). If curl F = 0 at each point of a region, then F is said to be irrotational in that region, since no circulation occurs about any point of the region
